en: WERNER : Women!... I don't mean yours: she is wonderful.
EUSTACHE : I have already had occasion to notice that you appreciate Béatrice.
WERNER, simply : Yes.
EUSTACHE : Besides, in her eyes you possess such prestige...
WERNER : What prestige? I would like to know?...
EUSTACHE : Music. Exile. Above all, exile. If I were to repeat to her what you have just told me, her admiration for you would know no bounds.
WERNER : Then don't tell her. Besides, it is better that way.
EUSTACHE : And so modest with it all.
WERNER : Eustache, you are irritating, you know... I've been wanting to tell you for several days now... It will be better if we no longer live here.
EUSTACHE : What's gotten into you?
WERNER : You can see for yourself. I am a little sad, I'm not angry. There is something wrong here. I can't quite understand it, but I know it. Es stimmt nicht mehr.
EUSTACHE : That is out of the question.
WERNER : Still, one must look at the truth.
EUSTACHE : I am not aware that it has ever frightened me.
WERNER, without answering : You have... you have been a wonderful friend. You must be able to remain one. For that, I have to leave.
EUSTACHE : In the first place, where would you go?
WERNER : We will find something. I still have a little money in Switzerland. Fortunately I took precautions. Gisela doesn't know about it either, for that matter.
EUSTACHE : Perhaps you ought to show a little more trust in her.

WERNER : I have to spare her. All these circumstances are too much for her. I know her. I already knew her when I married her. She has always been very sheltered. She is not, how do you say? a fruit grown in the open wind. So one cannot tell the whole truth. One doesn't have the right.
EUSTACHE : I wonder if that is the way to help her... grow up.
WERNER : Before growing up, one must exist. Gisela is someone who exists with difficulty. She is not like your wife. (Eustache stirs.) I beg your pardon. I didn't mean to hurt you. (A silence.)

EUSTACHE : At the bottom of all this there is only a misunderstanding. You would cause both of us great grief by going off to live heaven knows where. In the first place, I thought that in Paris you hoped to sing in concerts.
WERNER : It's possible.
EUSTACHE : Then this is hardly the moment to go off and live in the country. And I can just see you from here in some furnished room, squalid, dark, with wretched food.
WERNER : One can find a boarding house...
EUSTACHE : No. (Werner laughs softly.) Why are you laughing? Besides, I really wonder what we would say to Béatrice.
WERNER : She would understand already.
EUSTACHE : What? There is nothing to understand.
WERNER : All these words are useless. To begin with, we had always agreed that we would only stay for a few weeks... I can always look to see if I find something... (He looks out the window.)
EUSTACHE : Obviously I cannot prevent you. But I certainly hope...
WERNER : Someone has just entered the garden... Madame Heuzard...
EUSTACHE, astonished : Gertrude?...
WERNER : I'll leave you. Besides, I must write to Switzerland about this recital... Give me your hand, Eustache.
EUSTACHE, slightly moved : What a child you are! (They shake hands; Werner exits to the left.)
[SCENE VI]
EUSTACHE : What is it?

GERTRUDE : I tried to phone you earlier. No one answered... I remembered you had no classes on Wednesday afternoon. I came on the off chance. I'm frozen. Do you mind if I close the window? Is your wife here?
EUSTACHE : I don't think she has gone out. Do you want me to...
GERTRUDE : On the contrary, I need to speak with you alone. Here it is. You know well enough that I dislike grand speeches. I've decided to end it all.
EUSTACHE : With what?
GERTRUDE : With everything. To end it... Well?
EUSTACHE : You can't be serious?

GERTRUDE : Do I look like I'm joking? You might well suspect that I've never cared much for life; it has always struck me as a rather dirty joke. I told you that living at my brother's had become intolerable. They are petty bourgeois whose stinginess is rivaled only by their hypocrisy. On top of that, she has a bigotry bordering on imbecility. So, you understand, I arranged to be there as little as possible. But a woman can hardly spend all eternity in cafés. I loathe the cinema, and besides, it costs money. It so happens there is an interior decorator in the building whom I got to know, a well-built fellow, not stupid, a pretty decent sort. He invited me up to his place. I went... well, it didn't take long; and I regret nothing. Only, I don't know, we couldn't be bothered to take precautions. And I'm pregnant.
EUSTACHE : Can't he marry you?

GERTRUDE : Out of the question. He wouldn't want to. Nor would I. Besides, he's more or less living with a Russian woman, some kind of neurotic wreck; I'm convinced she shoots up, and I told him so. Since that day we haven't seen each other. Only, you understand, I don't want this brat...
EUSTACHE : But still, once you have been reinstated, it seems to me...

GERTRUDE : In the first place, there's nothing new on that score. On the contrary. From what I've been able to gather, the report is as unfavorable as can be. They want to make an example of me. And even assuming... you know my views on the subject. With my husband there wasn't much danger... But I always did whatever was necessary to keep my peace of mind on that front... My first thought, once I was sure, was to get rid of it... But then I thought it over. That doesn't appeal to me at all. I have no confidence in it. I have no wish to end up crippled.
EUSTACHE : I can't quite grasp...
GERTRUDE : It's so much simpler. When a business is botched, you just drop it. You shouldn't cling on.
EUSTACHE : Life is not a "business".

GERTRUDE : No big words, please; I thought we agreed on despising humbug; you know what I mean by that. One must try to be logical with oneself all the same. In short, there are two questions to ask, and no more: what do I lose? who will miss me? The second isn't very important, and we can dispose of it in two words. Absolutely no one. Oh yes, you're very kind, it will affect you, but you'll get used to it very quickly, I guarantee you. Deep down my brother will be greatly relieved, because I cost him money; and as for my sister-in-law, she'll be torn between the satisfaction of being rid of me and the fury of having a suicide in the family.
EUSTACHE : This makes no sense. First of all, how can you be sure of losing nothing?

GERTRUDE : It's enough that I have a very clear feeling about it. What do you expect me to become? Streetwalking has no appeal for me; and besides, wanting it isn't enough. And then there are diseases: very troublesome. Already with my fellow I had a scare. Nothing serious. But it was enough for me.
EUSTACHE : The child... if you couldn't bring yourself to keep it with you... someone could be found to take care of it.
GERTRUDE : Why not Public Assistance?
EUSTACHE : No, not Public Assistance. It wouldn't be difficult.

GERTRUDE : You, I see what you're leading up to... Well, no! that disgusts me... And besides, can anyone answer for themselves? Once the kid is here, maybe I'll get attached to it, who knows? and if I give it up, maybe one day I'll regret it; I'll want it back. It will lead to no end of complications... I don't understand why you're making such an impossible face.
EUSTACHE : I cannot explain it.
GERTRUDE : You ought to try.
EUSTACHE : I can't even take it in...
GERTRUDE : The truth is that you are infinitely too sentimental. I think life is bookkeeping, nothing else... But really, please, don't look so devastated.
EUSTACHE : Besides, why did you come to announce your decision to me?

GERTRUDE : First of all, I had a letter to hand you in person. Yes, you will find certain instructions in it regarding my papers... And then, I don't know. Let's say I felt like seeing you one more time. Does that make you angry?

EUSTACHE : I cannot help wondering if there isn't an element of illusion in all this... or if you aren't yielding instead to a kind of vertigo. Let me speak, won't you? After all, if we obtained your reinstatement, nothing would prevent the child from being born. Besides, if you absolutely insisted on having an abortion, someone could, I suppose, put you in touch with a specialist who would operate without risk.
GERTRUDE : Allow me. I repeat to you that at the Ministry they are as ill-disposed toward me as possible...
EUSTACHE : Yes, but I had proof just earlier that I have support there.
GERTRUDE : Congratulations. But they wouldn't work in my favor, you can be sure of that.
EUSTACHE : If that is the case, I refuse the offer that was just made to me.
GERTRUDE : That defies common sense. What surprises me is simply that you stand so well with those reactionaries.
EUSTACHE : Surely you aren't going to imagine that I gave pledges...

GERTRUDE : I'm sure of the opposite. But that's precisely what is so marvelous in your career: your very integrity succeeds for you. I've noticed that two or three times: independence and selflessness can become gold mines. Provided, of course, that one has connections.
EUSTACHE : I ask you to clarify those insinuations.
GERTRUDE : Come now, we're not going to quarrel. For me, after all, it wouldn't be of much importance. But you, I know you, you'd find a way to blame yourself.
EUSTACHE, to himself : This is intolerable.
[SCENE VII]
THE SAME, BÉATRICE.
BÉATRICE : I had no idea you were here. Why didn't you let me know?
GERTRUDE : It's my fault. I didn't want him to disturb you. Besides, I had a somewhat confidential word to say to him.
BÉATRICE : Very well.
GERTRUDE : Concerning a third party.
EUSTACHE, bluntly : That's not true. Do you know what she just announced to me?

GERTRUDE : Oh no, Eustache, please. If you want me to carry out my plan this very evening, you have only to continue. Once I'm gone, say whatever you like. I take it you are one of those men who unload themselves relentlessly onto their wives.
BÉATRICE : Fortunately.
GERTRUDE : But in my presence, not a word.
EUSTACHE : So you are going to leave, inflicting on me this worry, this agony... it is hellish.
GERTRUDE : No grand words, please.
EUSTACHE : Béatrice, hold her back.
BÉATRICE : What do you want me to say to her? I know nothing about any of this.
EUSTACHE : It isn't hard to guess.
GERTRUDE : Remember what I told you.
EUSTACHE, to Béatrice : You are taking on a terrible responsibility right now.
BÉATRICE : I am?
GERTRUDE : Farewell. (She exits quickly.)
EUSTACHE : Gertrude!
BÉATRICE, holding him back : Let her go.
EUSTACHE, breaking away violently : You are mad!
GERTRUDE, from outside : Don't get worked up. I'm not yet entirely sure I wasn't just pulling your leg...
EUSTACHE : What? What do you mean?
GERTRUDE : I'll telephone you tomorrow morning. (She disappears.)
[SCENE VIII]
BÉATRICE, calmly : You see...
EUSTACHE : She came to tell me of her intention to kill herself.
BÉATRICE : I understood that well enough.
EUSTACHE : Does that leave you cold?
BÉATRICE : You heard just now...
EUSTACHE : Does that count? That was only to reassure me.
BÉATRICE : What delicacy! What exquisite behavior!
EUSTACHE : Béatrice, do you realize?
BÉATRICE, keeping her composure : You are beside yourself...
EUSTACHE : Earlier, while she was speaking... it was the very face of despair I had before me.
BÉATRICE : Oh no, you are mistaken... To suffer, one must love.
EUSTACHE : Suffering kills love.
BÉATRICE : That is not true.
EUSTACHE : The worst of all is not pain, it's worry. One simply has nothing left with which to love. One is hollowed out. There is nothing left. A moral dysentery. It is appalling.
BÉATRICE, without answering : If she had the slightest intention of killing herself, she would not have come to inform you of it.
EUSTACHE : What was her motive then?
BÉATRICE : I have already told you what I thought of her feelings for you. I will add that she cannot stand me, naturally.
EUSTACHE : What does that have to do with it?
BÉATRICE : She seems to me to have an unerring instinct for what can, I don't say merely hurt you, but threaten our union, our happiness.
EUSTACHE : Say rather our comfort. It's true that comes to the same thing. At least for you.
BÉATRICE : Ungrateful man! Do you think poverty would have frightened me?
EUSTACHE : You know what conditionals are worth!...
BÉATRICE : It is our marriage that you cannot forgive me for,
EUSTACHE : I wanted you given to me without a dowry, don't forget that...
BÉATRICE : Always that wretched dowry! What did it matter? What pettiness to keep harping on this question of money! As if that mattered!
EUSTACHE : If your parents had listened to me...
BÉATRICE : They did you the honor of believing you were above such pettiness.
EUSTACHE : Your father never missed an opportunity to humiliate me.
BÉATRICE : But don't you understand, Eustache, that the origin of all this is in you, deep inside yourself—in everything you will never admit to yourself...
EUSTACHE : What do you mean?
BÉATRICE : It is something one can scarcely express, first of all because it is too... (low) too painful.
EUSTACHE : One question. It wasn't Werner by any chance who put these preposterous ideas into your head?
BÉATRICE : I did not need Werner to understand you.
EUSTACHE : You are dodging the question. Earlier, when you broke off so abruptly, you were talking about me. Do you admit it?
BÉATRICE : I have no reason to deny it.
EUSTACHE : Then why did he claim that you were questioning him about Germany?
BÉATRICE : He wanted to...
EUSTACHE : Spare me.
BÉATRICE : Can you hold it against him that he knows you are vulnerable? And does not the resentment you show him right now prove just how clearly he saw?
EUSTACHE : You did not speak like this before he came.
BÉATRICE : I assure you: he had nothing to do with what happened.
EUSTACHE : What happened?
[SCENE IX]
THE SAME, WERNER.
WERNER : I beg your pardon. Could you give me a foreign stamp? This letter must go out.
BÉATRICE : There should be some here in the blotter. (She searches.)

EUSTACHE : I might as well let you know... Béatrice had to admit just now that you didn't tell me the truth earlier. I simply take note of it... In the future I would prefer it if people concerned themselves a little less with me around here. This excessive solicitude is rather... wearisome. (A silence.)
WERNER, softly : I found an address in my wallet that someone gave me in Switzerland. I will go tomorrow and see if there is room.
BÉATRICE : What?
EUSTACHE : Don't force me to repeat in front of Béatrice what I told you earlier. I am no weathercock. But living together implies...
WERNER : Perhaps you mean sacrifices?
EUSTACHE : Not even that. A certain mutual respect, or more precisely, a discretion...
BÉATRICE : Eustache, you don't realize what you are saying!
EUSTACHE, in a different tone : I have thought it over. I am absolutely determined to refuse this flattering promotion.

BÉATRICE : I wonder when you had time to think about it. You haven't been alone for a second since the telephone call from the Ministry... Or rather, yes, I see... it is the plainest outcome of that visit...
EUSTACHE : Take care.
BÉATRICE : You will do exactly as you wish; I have no pretension whatsoever of influencing you.

WERNER, gently : You are wrong. You must not let him... how do you say? trap himself. I know nothing of such matters, but it seems to me this promotion only becomes important if you refuse it. That is, you give it importance, you adopt an attitude of which you may very quickly become the prisoner.
EUSTACHE, curtly : I don't understand. And since you say yourself that you know nothing about it...
WERNER, to Béatrice : You must not let him slide down that slope. It is as though he wanted to win back something he had never lost.
EUSTACHE : You would oblige me greatly by not treating me as though I weren't here.
WERNER : But you are absent. You are no longer with us. That is the misfortune.
EUSTACHE : Do you think I don't know why you feel entitled to take such superior airs with me? Your position is advantageous, and you know how to exploit it.
[SCENE X]
THE SAME, GISELA.
GISELA : What is going on?

EUSTACHE : In your place, perhaps after all I would not behave any differently. Yet it seems to me... but who can say? Delicacy, not to mention generosity: I suppose that is a luxury one cannot afford when one has severed all one's ties, as you have.
WERNER : Be careful.
EUSTACHE : And now that you have this magnificent gesture to your credit...
WERNER : You are completely mad.
GISELA : What magnificent gesture?
WERNER, trying to drown out Eustache's voice : That means nothing; he's talking nonsense.
EUSTACHE : Dare to maintain that.
BÉATRICE : Eustache, you are no longer master of yourself... (To Werner.) Forgive him.
EUSTACHE : That's right. Rely a little on his nobility of soul. (To Gisela.) Do you know who Wetzinger is?
WERNER : You are about to do something foul, Eustache!
GISELA : Wetzinger? The impresario? What does that have to do with anything?
BÉATRICE : Eustache, I beg you to listen to me. It is that Heuzard woman who has made you lose your head.
EUSTACHE : As if you were mistress of yourself at this moment!
GISELA : Is Wetzinger in Paris?
EUSTACHE : Ask your husband.
GISELA : Werner! I want to know... is he in Paris?
WERNER : Don't scream like a madwoman; you're splitting my head.
BÉATRICE, to Eustache : I guarantee you she never had any thought of killing herself.
GISELA : Did someone kill themselves?
EUSTACHE : I consider that Werner owes you an explanation. (Meanwhile Werner has gone to the piano; he shakes his head sorrowfully while playing a few notes.)

GISELA : Werner, stop strumming on the piano, it's exasperating... (Werner softly strikes a few chords.) Did you see Wetzinger? You don't want to answer me? Very well then, I know now. (To Eustache.) Did he tell you?... (To Werner.) Did he propose that you return to Germany? We could have gone back to Germany?... But perhaps it isn't too late yet.
WERNER : Wetzinger has left.
GISELA : You admit that he offered you...
WERNER : I told him no... irrevocably no.

GISELA, in a voice increasingly choked with sobs : You had no right... You are not alone... I am here too... I don't want to live here like a beggar... I have my family, my home, my own life... What do I care about politics?
BÉATRICE, going to her : Gisela, listen to me...

GISELA : I am not an idiot, I will not let myself be sacrificed... Werner! (He does not answer, but continues to strike chords, his eyes staring into the distance.) Ah! Rudolf is behind this again... I'm warning you... I will not spend my existence fighting a dead man... I didn't know I was married to a madman. I will leave, do you hear me... but not alone, there will be someone else... Ein Wahnsinniger... (She exits sobbing.) (A long silence.) (Eustache has sat down in the background and seems absorbed in reading a book he picked up from the table; the other two entirely ignore his presence.)
WERNER, without turning around : If there were only the living, Gisela, I think the earth would be utterly uninhabitable.
BÉATRICE : What did you say, Werner? I didn't understand. (Werner turns around, looks at her...)
WERNER, softly : Forgive me, Béatrice.
